f.claim: Serializing writes does not yet prevent one clone from silently replacing another clone's newer shared state, because mutation preconditions remain undefined.
f.location: CURRENT-DESIGN.md, State and reconciliation; DESIGN-NOTES.md:149-160
f.evidence: Current design explicitly says 'precise stale-edit/precondition semantics still need design'; notes say 'Serial execution prevents simultaneous writes, but does not by itself detect a stale whole-file replacement computed by a caller.' Failure story: two clones read a seat's instructions, independently revise different concerns, and enqueue complete replacement text. Both requests serialize successfully, but the second removes the first's decision. This is an acknowledged unresolved contract, not a contradiction or a claim that the design promises implementation readiness.

f.claim: The closure-to-retirement rule lacks the cascade and unavailable-observation contract needed to avoid retiring the wrong scope during ordinary workspace recovery.
f.location: CURRENT-DESIGN.md, State and reconciliation; DESIGN-NOTES.md:147,157,197-198
f.evidence: Current design makes closing a live pane/tab/workspace retire corresponding graph objects, while explicitly leaving 'Exact cascading closure and external cleanup contracts' open. Notes additionally leave the last-pane/containing-tab behavior and closure versus unavailable observation unspecified. Failure story: a last-pane close or workspace disappearance is represented as multiple observations; the implementation archives a containing seat/team or cleans up participants whose intended lifecycle was not actually resolved. Accepted best-effort missed manual actions do not choose the scope of an action that was observed.

votes.evidence: Narrowed to unavailable observation versus closure. CURRENT-DESIGN.md:15-18 says observed Herdr changes feed the graph writer, committed intent drives reconciliation, and closing a live pane/tab/workspace retires corresponding graph objects; it explicitly leaves closure contracts open. DESIGN-NOTES.md:147 expressly says reliable distinction between closure and unavailable observation needs specification; :157 notes an incomplete snapshot is insufficient evidence of deliberate closure. Concrete path: a formerly live tab is temporarily absent from a check, the unspecified classifier treats that absence as a manual close, the writer archives its seat, and latest-intent reconciliation (:179; CURRENT-DESIGN.md:16) drives retirement/cleanup even when availability returns. That leaves a still-intended responsibility archived and possibly changes thread participation, contradicting HERDR-GRAPH-VISION.md:9,33,90-94's organizational continuity and requirement to distinguish deliberate changes from incomplete observations. This is a contract gap, not a claim of actual implementation data loss. The separate last-pane cascade concern is acknowledged as open at DESIGN-NOTES.md:147 but is not needed for this demonstrated failure.

(a) No equivalent settled cascade or closure-evidence rule appears in the four artifacts: CURRENT-DESIGN.md:18 explicitly leaves cascading closure and external cleanup unspecified; DESIGN-NOTES.md:147 explicitly leaves last-pane/containing-tab behavior and closure-versus-unavailability unresolved. DESIGN-NOTES.md:157 says an incomplete snapshot is insufficient, but labels that section 'proposed for discussion, not yet approved'; HERDR-GRAPH-VISION.md:94 likewise states the desired distinction while leaving exact matching/conflict policy open. (b) Best-effort missed manual actions are accepted (DESIGN-NOTES.md:180), but that tradeoff does not settle the scope or classification of an observed change. (c) Pane/tab/workspace retirement is in current scope (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:18), including closure undo (DESIGN-NOTES.md:278). (d) Misclassifying temporary unavailability as closure, or a last-pane close as seat retirement, changes durable lifecycle and thread cleanup (DESIGN-NOTES.md:147), so this is material. Narrow finding: an acknowledged design contract gap, not evidence that implementation currently loses data or that every missed action must be recovered.

Confirmed, narrowed to the unresolved decision rule rather than an absence of any safeguard. CURRENT-DESIGN.md:18 adopts retirement on live pane/tab/workspace closure and explicitly leaves cascading closure and external cleanup unspecified. DESIGN-NOTES.md:147 expressly leaves last-pane/containing-tab behavior and reliable closure-versus-unavailable-observation distinction open; :157 proposes that an incomplete snapshot cannot prove deliberate closure and that graph-issued closures need correlation, but this is labeled an unapproved consequence, not a complete rule. Full-text search of all four artifacts for close/closure, retire/archive, cascade, unavailable/missing/snapshot, ambiguity, and recovery found directional safeguards at DESIGN-NOTES.md:125,157,166,197-198 and HERDR-GRAPH-VISION.md:33,92-94, yet no adopted evidence threshold or descendant-scope mapping. The missing contract is material to the stated requirement that ordinary manual Herdr changes feed graph state while preserving correct organizational identity (HERDR-GRAPH-VISION.md:33,54,94,139). A last-pane observation or transiently incomplete workspace view could otherwise be interpreted at the wrong scope; this is a prospective design risk, not a claim of actual data loss or a demand for perfect observation. The accepted best-effort allowance for missed actions (DESIGN-NOTES.md:180) does not settle classification of an observed ambiguous action.

f.claim: Automatic /seat bootstrap can create a fresh bound identity in the recovery pane before undo adopts that pane, with no contract for resolving that provisional identity.
f.location: DESIGN-NOTES.md:193,238,263-265,272-274; CURRENT-DESIGN.md, Bootstrap and system-duty seats / Undo
f.evidence: Session-start instructions can automatically run /seat; unbound context may create a seat through a plan. Undo is a separate CLI because automatic matching/creation conflicts with restoring a previous object into a fresh location, and the command's current pane must be adopted into the restoration. Failure story: after accidentally closing a seat, the user opens the requested fresh tab/agent; boot creates a new seat and channels before the user asks for recovery. Undo now encounters an already bound pane. The design leaves unspecified whether adoption retires/reuses that provisional seat, transfers its new history, or refuses restoration, and how it avoids a leftover identity even though it promises to avoid a leftover recovery pane.

votes.evidence: Conditional but supported path: close established seat S, which archives it (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:18); open fresh tab/pane P and agent to undo the closure (DESIGN-NOTES.md:232). Session-start instructions may run /seat (DESIGN-NOTES.md:238; CURRENT-DESIGN.md:30), and unbound /load may propose creation as well as resurrection/rebind (DESIGN-NOTES.md:193). If that plan creates fresh seat N and binds P before the user requests undo, the dedicated CLI then must adopt its current P into restored S (DESIGN-NOTES.md:263-265,272-274; CURRENT-DESIGN.md:46). The stated plan does not say whether N is retired, retained, or transferred, nor how N's new native-session history and thread relationships follow the rebind; the listed open details cover multi-object adoption and dependency conflicts but do not resolve this case (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:49). Thus a permitted ordinary boot order leaves the promised concrete adoption/restoration plan underdetermined and can leave a second live identity or incorrectly scoped history. This is a material recovery-contract gap, not a claim that every boot creates N or that data loss has occurred.

(a) No equivalent resolution found: DESIGN-NOTES.md:193 permits create/resurrect/rebind for unbound context, :238 enables session-start /seat prompting, while :263 explicitly recognizes /seat matching/creation conflicts with restoration; :265 and :273 promise adoption of the undo command's current pane but give no disposition for a fresh seat already bound there. Generic conflict/repair planning (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:49; DESIGN-NOTES.md:289) does not settle retire/reuse/transfer of that seat and its channels/history. (b) Best-effort missed observations and open multi-object mapping are accepted, but neither explicitly accepts a leftover provisional identity in this ordinary recovery path. (c) Closure undo and pane adoption are initial scope (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:46-47), so this is in scope. (d) If startup /seat creates a seat before the user runs the separate undo CLI, adopting its pane for the resurrected seat leaves the new durable seat identity's fate undefined, potentially breaking clean recovery and attribution; no actual data loss is established. Narrow finding to this timing/identity interaction, not a general demand for atomic undo.

Premises hold, with a conditional trigger: DESIGN-NOTES.md:238 and CURRENT-DESIGN.md:30 permit session-start /seat; DESIGN-NOTES.md:193 allows an unbound context to propose a create/resurrect/rebind plan, so creation is possible but not inevitable. DESIGN-NOTES.md:263 explicitly identifies automatic matching/creation as conflicting with restoration into a fresh location; :265 and :273 require adopting the undo command's current pane. Full-text searches across all four artifacts for binding/rebind, resurrection, recovery/restore/undo, adoption, reuse, and retirement found no rule for a seat/clone already created in that pane before undo. Generic conflict repair at :289 and acknowledged open restoration details in CURRENT-DESIGN.md:49 do not specify disposition of its independent seat ID, channels, or history. If bootstrap has created that identity, adopting the same pane into the archived seat cannot be planned unambiguously while preserving identity/provenance (DESIGN-NOTES.md:300-302) and avoiding a leftover recovery pane (:265). This materially affects the stated closure-recovery experience; it is an acknowledged design-stage gap, with no claim of observed data loss.

f.claim: Transcript coverage has no settled rule for concurrent or out-of-order results, so late completion can make the recovery summary represent less transcript than an earlier completion.
f.location: CURRENT-DESIGN.md, Bootstrap and system-duty seats; DESIGN-NOTES.md:248,255-259
f.evidence: The summarizer accepts additional work without waiting for earlier summaries; resumed transcripts append processing work; completion reports carry processed-through coverage and a summary path. The notes explicitly leave 'concurrent or out-of-order result handling' open. Failure story: a request covering a resumed transcript finishes first, then an older request overwrites the same artifact or becomes the current result. The graph's summary pointer or watermark now exposes an incomplete account as the usable recovery artifact. This is a concrete acknowledged design gap rather than a requirement to merge arbitrary summaries automatically.

votes.evidence: Acknowledged gap, narrowed to current-result selection (physical artifact overwrite is not specified). DESIGN-NOTES.md:247-259 permits concurrent requests and newly appended transcript work, requires explicit results with transcript identity, processed-through position and summary path, and expressly leaves concurrent/out-of-order result handling open; CURRENT-DESIGN.md:32-34 repeats that contract. Concrete sequence: request A processes transcript through position 100; after resume request B processes through 150. B completes first, A later. If the unresolved completion rule treats the last arrival as current, the recovery reference regresses to coverage 100 despite completed coverage 150. Nothing specified requires choosing the greatest valid coverage or keeping a later-coverage result current. That breaks the stated purpose of indexed transcript summaries for recovery (DESIGN-NOTES.md:228-241; HERDR-GRAPH-VISION.md:37,139), while the explicit processed-through field makes the missing ordering rule consequential. This is a design gap before implementation, not evidence of existing data loss.

(c) Mechanical transcript processing/indexing is expressly in scope (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:10,32-34). (d) A later-arriving result for an earlier transcript portion could be exposed as the latest usable summary without the resumed portion, impairing the stated recovery/continuity goal (HERDR-GRAPH-VISION.md:37,139). Narrowing: the spec does not promise a single current pointer or allow overwriting a shared artifact; those are illustrative failure paths, not established behavior. The material missing rule is how graph represents usable coverage when results complete out of order. This is an acknowledged design gap, not an implementation claim.

CURRENT-DESIGN.md:32-34 approves durable transcript requests, concurrent dispatch, coverage/output references and resumed work, then explicitly leaves out-of-order results open. DESIGN-NOTES.md:248,256-259 confirms the main occupant need not wait, completion includes transcript identity, processed-through position and summary path, and no ordering rule is settled. Full-text search of all four artifacts for summary/result/coverage/recovery and equivalent handling found no monotonic current-result selection, artifact versioning, or overwrite rule. Narrowing: neither a single summary pointer nor shared-path overwrite is specified, so regression is a plausible failure mode of the acknowledged contract gap, not an established behavior or actual data loss. f.claim: The transcript workflow specifies activation when no occupant exists but leaves pending-request recovery undefined when an occupant remains present and stops making progress.
f.location: DESIGN-NOTES.md:247-259; CURRENT-DESIGN.md, Bootstrap and system-duty seats
f.evidence: Graph activates an unoccupied summarizer, reuses an existing occupant without requiring it to be idle, and preserves pending requests after crashes. Instructions tell the occupant to dispatch subagents and report results; the durable contract currently distinguishes requests and explicit completion but defines no stalled/in-progress/failure reporting or reassignment policy for a still-running occupant. Failure story: the summarizer dispatches processing that never reports, remains present accepting messages, and requests remain indefinitely pending while successors wait for recovery summaries. Durable discoverability prevents disappearance but does not settle how this case is detected or repaired. A recovery policy can remain ordinary agent practice; no plugin worker pool or periodic model wake is required by this finding.

votes.evidence: Concrete path: graph posts a durable transcript request to a present summarizer (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:32-34; DESIGN-NOTES.md:250,258); its helper stalls without a completion report (DESIGN-NOTES.md:248,251,256); graph therefore leaves the request pending and discoverable (DESIGN-NOTES.md:256-257). The demonstration stops there: the approved contract requires durable requests, explicit completion, and recovery after occupant loss, but states no deadline or automatic stall detection for a still-present occupant. The notes place dispatch/reply behavior in role instructions and reject a plugin worker pool (DESIGN-NOTES.md:248-250,258); CURRENT-DESIGN.md:54 explicitly leaves crash/retry behavior for further design. Thus indefinite pending work is a real operational risk, but this story does not reach a contradiction of a stated transcript-workflow guarantee. It would require an additional liveness requirement to confirm this finding.

(a) Equivalent mechanism: none found. DESIGN-NOTES.md:247-259 specifies activation only when unoccupied, durable pending requests, explicit completion, and result coverage; it leaves retry/deduplication open. Graph-operation reminders/reassignment at DESIGN-NOTES.md:150-189 are expressly limited to structural/relationship requests (187), so they do not cover transcript processing. (b) Accepted contract: role instructions own dispatch and reporting (248,258), and no recurring model wake is selected (240), but neither accepts indefinitely stalled transcript work as an outcome. (c) Scope: mechanical transcript indexing and processing requests are now in scope (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:10,39-43; DESIGN-NOTES.md:241,255-258); a stall policy could remain ordinary agent practice. (d) Materiality: if a still-present occupant dispatches a subagent that never reports, the request remains pending without a defined detection/recovery path; the intended transcript-processing result and coverage record (DESIGN-NOTES.md:256-257) may never appear. This confirms only the missing stalled-request recovery contract, not a requirement for a plugin worker pool or periodic model wake.

DESIGN-NOTES.md:247-258 approves activation only for an unoccupied summarizer, reuse of an existing occupant without requiring idleness, durable pending requests, and explicit completion distinct from dispatch. CURRENT-DESIGN.md:32-34 repeats that contract and :54 names summarizer crash/retry as open. Full-text checks for stalled/stuck/hung/unresponsive work, timeout/heartbeat/progress, failure reporting, reminder, retry, reassignment, and monitoring across all four artifacts found no policy for a present occupant whose dispatched work never completes. CURRENT-DESIGN.md:17 and DESIGN-NOTES.md:170-189 cover failed graph mutations and external reconciliation, not transcript-processing request liveness; SOFTWARE-FACTORY-VISION.md:77 covers a separate instance monitoring recipe. Narrowly, a request can remain visibly pending indefinitely while the summarizer is present, preventing the transcript result/coverage promised in DESIGN-NOTES.md:255-258 and weakening cross-session continuity (HERDR-GRAPH-VISION.md:137-139). This is an acknowledged design-stage gap, not a claim of actual data loss or a requirement for a plugin worker pool or periodic model wake.

f.claim: Asynchronous transcript processing has no defined source-availability contract, so durable requests may outlive the input needed to fulfill them.
f.location: DESIGN-NOTES.md:241,251,255-259; CURRENT-DESIGN.md, Bootstrap and system-duty seats; CURRENT-DESIGN.md:34,54; DESIGN-NOTES.md:253-259
f.evidence:
Source 7 (premortem, GAP): Graph tracks native transcript references and processed-through coverage, triggers work after session closure, and persists requests across occupant loss. The design does not state who ensures that the referenced input remains readable, how it identifies a truncated/replaced source, or how an unavailable transcript becomes a terminal repairable result. Failure story: a pending summary is retried after its source was moved or removed, and durable request persistence alone cannot reconstruct it. This does not assert any particular harness retention behavior or require graph to own a transcript archive; the missing contract could instead expose source-unavailable status and a documented recovery limitation.

Source 11 (completeness, GAP): New error-case gap within the acknowledged unfinished request contract: results reference 'transcript identity, processed-through position, and summary path'; resumed transcripts can append work and pending requests survive crashes. The only explicit result described is completion with coverage. No retained snapshot requirement, input-unavailable outcome, or reduced-coverage disposition is stated. This matters even if transcript retention remains harness-owned: the graph must avoid representing unreadable coverage as completed or leaving such requests indistinguishable from retryable pending work. It is not a claim that native transcripts are guaranteed to disappear.

f.claim: Cancellation does not specify how outstanding reconciliation is stopped when the cancelled request has already committed the desired state that keeps generating its effects.
f.location: CURRENT-DESIGN.md: State and reconciliation; DESIGN-NOTES.md:177–189; DESIGN-NOTES.md:179,185–189; CURRENT-DESIGN.md — State and reconciliation.
f.evidence:
Source 17 (failure-mode, GAP): The approved policy is to follow 'latest committed intent' and retry transient failures automatically. Separately, cancellation 'ends obsolete work/reminders' without claiming that effects happened or were undone. Consider a committed activation whose Herdr creation fails, followed by cancellation while desired activation remains current: a normal reconciliation still sees an absent desired pane and can issue the same creation again. Cancelling a request must have some specified relationship to desired state, effect suppression, or a superseding mutation; none is selected. This is an unsealed cancellation contract, not evidence that cancellation must undo already-performed effects.

Source 30 (domain:distributed-state-reconciliation, GAP): Reconciliation follows latest committed intent, while approved cancellation 'ends obsolete work/reminders' and does not imply effects were undone. Consider committed activation intent whose pane creation fails while Herdr is unavailable. The user cancels the unresolved graph request, then Herdr recovers. If cancellation only ends the request/retries, the ordinary periodic intent-versus-runtime check still finds the absent desired pane and creates it. If cancellation suppresses the intent, the design needs to say what desired lifecycle/relationship is now authoritative and which already-completed effects remain. The same ambiguity occurs when the requested desired state comes from a live template. This needs a cancellation state transition or a clearly bounded cancellation scope, not automatic rollback of external effects.

f.claim: Automatic activation of an unoccupied summarizer has no defined precedence against an explicit retirement of that same seat.
f.location: CURRENT-DESIGN.md: State and reconciliation and Bootstrap and system-duty seats; DESIGN-NOTES.md:147,179,247–258
f.evidence: Manual tab closure retires the corresponding seat, reconciliation follows latest committed intent, and graph activates an 'unoccupied summarizer' through ordinary activation whenever transcript processing is needed. The notes expressly say this does not establish auto-resurrection for arbitrary retired seats, but do not distinguish retired from dormant for the summarizer itself. A user closing the summarizer while transcript requests are pending therefore has no defined outcome: automatically resurrect the retired seat, leave requests discoverable, or use another seat. An ordinary activation operation does not by itself settle this precedence.

votes.evidence: Concrete path: (1) A summarizer has pending transcript work; pending requests survive occupant loss (DESIGN-NOTES.md:251,255-258; CURRENT-DESIGN.md:32-34). (2) The human closes its live tab. That observed closure commits retirement and archives the seat, rather than merely leaving an active seat without an occupant (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:16,18; DESIGN-NOTES.md:147,197-198). Its approved rule says to activate an unoccupied summarizer through ordinary activation before posting requests (DESIGN-NOTES.md:247,250,258; CURRENT-DESIGN.md:32). Applying that rule to the retired seat recreates/rehydrates it despite the later retirement intent, contrary to latest-committed-intent reconciliation (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:16; DESIGN-NOTES.md:179) and the promised distinction between retirement and dormancy (DESIGN-NOTES.md:102,197-198). Skipping activation instead leaves the approved automatic-processing rule inapplicable with no specified disposition beyond request discoverability. The design expressly limits any inference that all retired seats auto-resurrect (DESIGN-NOTES.md:250), but never resolves this summarizer-specific collision. Narrow finding: define lifecycle eligibility/precedence for a deliberately retired summarizer and its pending requests; it does not demand auto-resurrection or uninterrupted processing after retirement.

(a) No equivalent precedence rule found: CURRENT-DESIGN.md:16 says reconciliation follows latest committed intent, but does not decide whether transcript work creates new activation intent after retirement; :18 says manual tab closure retires the seat; :32 says an absent occupant is activated for processing. DESIGN-NOTES.md:197-198 distinguishes never-activated/active/retired lifecycle, while :247-250 and :258 approve activation of an 'unoccupied summarizer' without defining whether that includes retired. (b) Best-effort missed observations (:179-180) do not resolve an observed/committed retirement, and :250 bounds auto-resurrection of arbitrary seats but does not settle the summarizer itself. (c) The question is within agreed mechanical transcript scope (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:10,32-34), not a request for general scheduling. (d) Material: after the user closes the summarizer tab with processing pending, automatic activation could recreate the deliberately retired seat, whereas suppression leaves pending requests with no specified processing path. The contract must define retirement versus summarizer activation precedence; this is an acknowledged lifecycle detail, not an implementation defect or data-loss claim.

DESIGN-NOTES.md:197 distinguishes never-activated absence from retirement; :247 and :258 approve unqualified activation for an unoccupied summarizer, while :250 explicitly leaves the retired/unoccupied boundary unresolved for arbitrary seats. DESIGN-NOTES.md:217 and CURRENT-DESIGN.md:24 protect locally retired template members from recreation, but neither states whether summarizer-triggered activation may override that retirement or must leave durable requests for reassignment/discovery. Thus a deliberately retired summarizer and pending/new transcript processing produce competing instructions without a specified outcome. Narrowing: this is a summarizer-specific lifecycle precedence gap, not a claim that retired seats generally auto-resurrect or that transcript requests are lost.

f.claim: Notification-driven whole-seat leave has no specified protection against a delayed agent instruction applying after a newer whole-seat join.
f.location: DESIGN-NOTES.md:13,57,177–179; CURRENT-DESIGN.md: Threads and policy; DESIGN-NOTES.md:13, 57, 179; CURRENT-DESIGN.md, State and reconciliation / Threads and policy
f.evidence:
Source 20 (failure-mode, GAP): Whole-seat leave removes intent and posts instructions telling other clones to leave individually, preserving pending work for unavailable clones. Individual leave can create a persistent clone opt-out, while latest-intent reconciliation stops obsolete effects. If a clone handles an old leave instruction after a later whole-seat join, acting on the instruction can remove current membership and potentially preserve that removal as a new opt-out. Stopping plugin retries does not retract instructions already stored in threads. The contract does not say how these agent-executed instructions carry intent revisions, are checked on execution, or are distinguished from a new voluntary clone leave. This is separate from the already acknowledged question of how new joins treat genuine existing opt-outs.

Source 33 (domain:agent-session-and-messaging-integration, GAP): Whole-seat leave removes participation intent and publishes an instruction for other clones to leave individually, preserving pending work for unavailable clones. Latest-intent reconciliation stops obsolete retries and checks intent before external actions, but the design does not carry a participation revision in already-published agent instructions or require recipients to recheck it before leaving. Reproduction at the contract level: clone B is unavailable during leave L; join J subsequently commits and B joins; B then consumes L and calls threads leave. The plugin's own latest-intent check cannot retract an agent's previously delivered command. Define how a recipient identifies an obsolete instruction and how its delayed completion is reconciled; this is separate from the acknowledged question about retaining clone opt-outs on a new join.

f.claim: The serialized writer has no specified crash-recovery boundary between journal admission, checkout mutation, Git commit, and recording operation completion.
f.location: CURRENT-DESIGN.md: State and reconciliation and Useful next design topics; DESIGN-NOTES.md:150–153,159
f.evidence: Mutation requests enter a durable journaled queue, one worker writes and commits, admission differs from completion, and reconciliation must use latest committed intent. A crash after files are changed but before Git commits leaves readable checkout contents ahead of committed intent; a crash after commit but before recording completion leaves the admitted request apparently unfinished. No selected recovery rule identifies the authoritative commit for an operation or prevents applying that mutation twice during replay. Serial execution eliminates simultaneous writers but not these interrupted transitions. The document explicitly lists mutation/journal contracts as future design; this finding identifies the concrete local failure boundary that remains to be settled rather than contradicting an implementation-readiness claim.

votes.evidence: Concrete interruption: a create-seat mutation is durably admitted, then the sole worker writes the shared checkout and crashes before Git commit; alternatively it commits and crashes before recording completion. Admission and completion are expressly distinct (DESIGN-NOTES.md:150), while graph state is Git-backed (DESIGN-NOTES.md:28) and reconciliation must follow latest committed intent (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:14-16; DESIGN-NOTES.md:179). On restart the first case leaves checkout files ahead of committed intent, and the second leaves an admitted request without a completion record. The design specifies neither how startup restores/ignores uncommitted checkout changes nor how a committed mutation is correlated to its journal request before replay or status reporting; mutation/journal contracts are explicitly next design work (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:53; DESIGN-NOTES.md:159 labels inspectable operation status a proposal). If the first checkout is treated as intent, reconciliation may drive an uncommitted seat; if the second request is replayed or left pending without commit correlation, the operation can be applied twice or reported unfinished. Either path conflicts with latest-committed-intent reconciliation and the stated visible, repairable partial-operation promise (HERDR-GRAPH-VISION.md:92-98,139). This is a material acknowledged design gap, not evidence that an implementation already loses data or that the draft claims implementation readiness (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:58).

The unknown-outcome rule in DESIGN-NOTES.md:174 is expressly for external effects, so it does not settle this local boundary. (b) The accepted best-effort/non-atomic tradeoff concerns external Herdr/threads effects (DESIGN-NOTES.md:152-153,179-180), not graph repository mutation integrity. The external-effect unknown-outcome rule (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:17; DESIGN-NOTES.md:174) does not specify local writer crash recovery. f.claim: The ordinary-seat summarizer design depends on a native occupant continuing to receive and act on durable thread requests across busy and idle states, but no end-to-end qualification of that service behavior is supplied.

f.evidence: The design says role instructions tell the summarizer to wait for requests, concurrently dispatch helpers, and report results; graph reuses an existing occupant without requiring it to be idle and activates only an absent occupant. Durable request storage proves recoverability, not that an existing native session consumes a newly arrived request after its prior turn finishes. The documents qualify launch flags but supply no corresponding busy/idle service trace. This finding asserts an unverified dependency, not that either supported harness cannot do it.

spike.question: Can an ordinary native summarizer service successive requests without a human continuation prompt or periodic model wake?
spike.cheapest_test: Use the existing threads integration and a minimal summarizer instruction file in each intended harness. Send one request while its previous subagent is active and another after its main turn has ended; then restart the occupant with one pending request. Record request receipt, dispatch and graph completion separately.
spike.kill_criteria: Reject the assumed unattended service contract for a harness if any request needs human prompting or an undeclared wake mechanism to progress. Keep the ordinary-seat model, but specify and prove the missing generic wake/resume path before relying on it.

votes.evidence: Narrow confirmation of an acknowledged service-contract assumption, not a claim that either harness fails. CURRENT-DESIGN.md:32-34 and DESIGN-NOTES.md:248-258 require graph to reuse an existing summarizer occupant, post durable thread requests without waiting for prior summaries, have that occupant accept/dispatch/report them, and recover pending requests after occupant loss; they select no periodic model wake. Reproduction if an occupant's main turn ends after request A: graph sees it still present, so does not take the approved absent-occupant activation path; it posts request B, but the text specifies no bridge from a newly durable thread message to a fresh native turn or continuing receive loop. B remains pending with no dispatch/result, contrary to the approved ordinary summarizer's request-processing role (DESIGN-NOTES.md:247-258; CURRENT-DESIGN.md:32-34). A request posted while a helper is active has the same unresolved receive boundary. Herdr does offer a possible external prompt surface: https://herdr.dev/docs/agent-automation/ says 'agent prompt submits text plus encoded Enter' and 'It can prompt an agent that is already working' (lines 132-138), but the design does not choose this or qualify a thread-driven equivalent. The cheapest closure is an end-to-end busy/idle/restart trace per intended harness, then specify a generic wake/resume path if needed. Durable pending storage prevents lost work; it does not itself make an existing idle occupant act.

(a) Equivalent search: CURRENT-DESIGN.md:32-34 and DESIGN-NOTES.md:247-259 specify ordinary activation only when no occupant runs, durable thread requests, role instructions to wait/dispatch, and pending-request discovery after crashes; none specifies how an existing occupant receives and acts on a request after its main turn ends. The reconciliation periodic checks in CURRENT-DESIGN.md:15 concern graph/Herdr state, and DESIGN-NOTES.md:240 and CURRENT-DESIGN.md:33 select no periodic model wake. (b) Best-effort missed manual observations (DESIGN-NOTES.md:179-180) are an accepted tradeoff, but stalled transcript requests are not; explicit completion and processed-through coverage are required (DESIGN-NOTES.md:255-258). (c) Mechanical transcript processing is current scope (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:10,32-34), though this is design-stage qualification, not an assertion that a harness cannot do it or a demand for production guarantees. (d) If a request arrives after an occupant's prior turn and nothing resumes it, the request persists without dispatch or completion, frustrating the selected processing workflow. Narrow finding: qualify/specify the generic delivery/resume path for busy and idle occupants before relying on unattended summarization. No claim about actual Codex/Claude runtime capability is made.

Narrowed to a design qualification gap, not a claim that either native harness lacks the capability. f.claim: The core continuity promise assumes agent-led retrieval and opaque memory practices recover live obligations accurately enough that replacing an occupant reduces human reconstruction, but that assumption has not been demonstrated.
f.location: HERDR-GRAPH-VISION.md:23,37,139; CURRENT-DESIGN.md:9-10,30; SOFTWARE-FACTORY-VISION.md:75-77
f.evidence: The first promised demonstration is recovering responsibility, outstanding work and evidence without a human rebuilding the story. Current design correctly leaves project work in Beads, sessions and wikis and has the agent discover applicable state itself, without a generated semantic brief. Those boundaries mean durable identity and transcript coverage alone do not establish correct recovery of outstanding obligations or current authorization. A factory recipe could provide that recovery; the four documents do not yet show evidence that one does. This is a product feasibility hypothesis, not a demand for graph to own a second commitment database.

spike.question: Can a replacement recover what matters from the chosen external records without the human repairing its account?
spike.cheapest_test: Prepare one small seat fixture containing an unfinished commitment, a superseded decision, an unresolved disagreement and a closed bead lacking acceptance, distributed across the intended stores. Give a fresh occupant only the planned /seat instructions and links. Compare its account and next action with a short human-authored answer key, and measure corrections and retrieval effort against the current manual workflow.
spike.kill_criteria: Do not claim the continuity recipe succeeds if the replacement misses a live obligation, treats obsolete direction as current, or requires as much human reconstruction as the baseline. Repair the instance retrieval/handoff practice before expanding the organization.

votes.evidence: (a) Equivalent recovery practice is present: a returning occupant uses durable instructions and linked records (HERDR-GRAPH-VISION.md:37,60-64); the approved load flow links relevant context and retrieves project work under instance instructions (DESIGN-NOTES.md:193-194), while the newer /seat decision has the agent read applicable state itself (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:30). The factory specifies recording assignments/decisions/remaining work for successors and a brief covering live commitments, authorization, evidence and recurring-job inspection (SOFTWARE-FACTORY-VISION.md:75-77,95-99). (b) The design explicitly treats a brief as orientation requiring fresh checks, and says transcript history alone cannot recover all commitments (DESIGN-NOTES.md:98,104); it makes no guarantee of perfect retrieval. (c) Graph deliberately does not own a second project-work or knowledge ledger (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:9-10; DESIGN-NOTES.md:186-194), so a demand for graph-held semantic obligations is outside scope. (d) Replacement continuity matters (HERDR-GRAPH-VISION.md:139), but this finding identifies only the absence of a completed empirical demonstration, which a design-stage proposal does not claim. The visions explicitly call continuity a future demonstration/product hypothesis and propose measurement (HERDR-GRAPH-VISION.md:139,145; SOFTWARE-FACTORY-VISION.md:147-157). A fixture trial is useful evaluation, but its absence is not a surviving material design gap.

f.claim: The concurrent-clone product scenario assumes a design decision in one conversation reaches and changes another conversation before it continues incompatible work, but the factory supplies no concrete decision-adoption practice to validate that outcome.
f.location: HERDR-GRAPH-VISION.md:29,110,139; SOFTWARE-FACTORY-VISION.md:35,105-109; CURRENT-DESIGN.md:37-40
f.evidence: The product explicitly offers design discussion in one clone while another executes and says relevant decisions are recorded and communicated. The texts correctly distinguish membership, receipt, and adoption and do not pretend shared seat identity means shared knowledge. Nevertheless the only proposed adoption practice is general lesson-sharing guidance; there is no worked case defining which current decision record an executing clone checks or how a conflicting in-flight action is reconsidered. The distinctive multi-clone benefit can otherwise produce concurrent work based on different accepted directions even when message transport is correct. This belongs to factory instructions and evaluation, not mandatory graph scheduling or locking.

spike.question: Does the proposed instance practice keep simultaneous design and execution coherent without making the human relay decisions?
spike.cheapest_test: Run two ordinary conversations for one seat. Let the executing clone begin a small reversible task, then have the human change an accepted requirement through the design clone. Use only planned records and threads, and observe whether the executing clone identifies the changed decision, reports already performed effects and adjusts remaining work.
spike.kill_criteria: Do not count concurrent clones as a demonstrated product advantage if the human must relay the decision or the executor reports completion against the superseded requirement. Specify and retest the instance decision-adoption practice.

votes.evidence: (a) An equivalent practice exists: SOFTWARE-FACTORY-VISION.md:33 says relevant decisions are recorded and communicated; :97 says to record decisions and distinguish receipt from agreement/acceptance; :107 says to preserve scoped findings in shared knowledge/instructions, notify affected peers, and have recipients assess, adjust, and report adoption or deferral. HERDR-GRAPH-VISION.md:29,35 supplies the same cross-conversation pattern, and DESIGN-NOTES.md:81-83 places behavioral rules in instance instructions. (b) HERDR-GRAPH-VISION.md:29 expressly disclaims shared context or instantaneous agreement; thus the asserted guarantee that the other clone changes course before continuing is outside the stated contract. (c) CURRENT-DESIGN.md:8 and DESIGN-NOTES.md:3 mark this as a design-stage draft; SOFTWARE-FACTORY-VISION.md:157 leaves exact instance practices to design, and HERDR-GRAPH-VISION.md:139-145 frames concurrent operation as a future demonstration, not a completed trial. (d) A worked in-flight requirement-change scenario would improve evaluation, but its absence does not establish a material contradiction or missing adoption practice. A completed empirical trial is not required of this draft.

f.claim: Cross-seat reload assumes a continuing native conversation can adopt a destination seat without carrying incompatible source-seat instructions or unfinished actions into that responsibility, and the design has not qualified that assumption.
f.location: CURRENT-DESIGN.md:19; DESIGN-NOTES.md:148
f.evidence: The adopted initial behavior detects a cross-tab move and requires destination-seat reload while preserving the old transcript/context. The notes explicitly acknowledge that the model does not forget its earlier instructions. They do not show how the initial reload behavior is expected to treat an unfinished source-seat task, a running helper, or conflicting old role instructions. This is a cooperative correctness concern, not an adversarial authorization claim, and it does not invalidate the deliberate decision to preserve history.

spike.question: Can the initial reload convention reliably separate preserved source history from destination responsibility?
spike.cheapest_test: Use two seats with intentionally different project paths and responsibilities. Move a native conversation after it has accepted a source task and dispatched a helper, then perform the proposed reload. Check its next tool target, attribution and treatment of the late helper result.
spike.kill_criteria: Reject transparent continuation for this case if it executes source work as destination work or attributes the late result to the new seat. Define a source-work handoff or fresh-session option for such moves; do not require erasing history.

votes.evidence: The strongest case is: a source seat accepts work, its pane moves, /seat reloads destination state, and a late helper result appears in the preserved transcript. CURRENT-DESIGN.md:19 and DESIGN-NOTES.md:148 explicitly retain that transcript while changing applicable graph state, so the situation is real. But the decisive step—continuing source work as destination work or falsely attributing the helper result—does not follow from either document. DESIGN-NOTES.md:148 expressly disclaims automatic forgetting; CURRENT-DESIGN.md:9 and DESIGN-NOTES.md:149 preserve session/transcript attribution, while DESIGN-NOTES.md:186-188 place project tasks in Beads/native sessions rather than graph. No stated contract says a move cancels an accepted source task or guarantees transparent execution of it by the destination seat. A source-work handoff convention may be useful, but this finding has no end-to-end contradiction of a stated requirement without assuming how an unspecified native session behaves.

(a) Equivalent search: /seat reads destination templates/rules and resolves binding (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:30; DESIGN-NOTES.md:193,238), and Beads/session attribution records prior work (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:9; DESIGN-NOTES.md:149,186), but none specifies what a moved conversation does with an accepted source-seat task, pending helper result, or conflicting old role instruction. (b) The accepted tradeoff is preserved transcript/context, explicitly without automatic forgetting (DESIGN-NOTES.md:148); this does not explicitly permit continuing source work under destination responsibility. (c) Cross-tab moves and eventual clone transfer are stated scope (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:19; DESIGN-NOTES.md:148). (d) The gap matters to promised continuity and truthful responsibility/attribution (HERDR-GRAPH-VISION.md:9,23,139; SOFTWARE-FACTORY-VISION.md:97): a move during unfinished source work has no defined handoff, defer, or fresh-session boundary before the same conversation acts as destination seat. Narrow finding: qualify this transition and in-flight work handling; preserving history itself is approved. This is a structural contract gap, not a claim that a native model will in fact obey stale instructions or misattribute a result, so no external capability premise is relied on.

Load-bearing premise fails: the adopted initial move requires a destination reload but explicitly retains the old transcript/context (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:19), and the detailed decision expressly says this does not claim the live model forgets prior instructions (DESIGN-NOTES.md:148). The reload reads current templates, rules and seat/clone configuration (DESIGN-NOTES.md:193); work commitments live in Beads/native sessions rather than graph state (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:9; DESIGN-NOTES.md:186), with general instructions to route out-of-responsibility work and preserve handoffs (SOFTWARE-FACTORY-VISION.md:87,97,117). Full-text search for move/reload/transfer/handoff/helper/unfinished-work equivalents found no cross-tab source-task handoff procedure, so that narrower edge case is open. But the finding alleges an unqualified assumption of clean adoption; the spec acknowledges preserved old context and does not promise transparent completion of in-flight source work. No external native-session behavior is needed for this judgment.

f.claim: The design gives writers serialization but gives readers no committed-snapshot contract, leaving /seat and reconciliation able to consume a partially applied multi-file graph mutation.
f.location: CURRENT-DESIGN.md — State and reconciliation; Bootstrap and system-duty seats. DESIGN-NOTES.md:150,164,238–239.
f.evidence: The shared checkout has one serialized writer; reconciliation is separate and must follow 'latest committed intent'; /seat's agent 'discovers/reads its applicable state directly.' A writer updating a template, seat overrides and renamed paths can expose its first file change before the remaining changes and Git commit. Neither writer serialization nor mutation preconditions specifies how concurrent readers choose one committed graph revision. A periodic reconciliation or /seat load during that interval can combine old overrides with new defaults, see transiently missing bindings, or drive an effect from intent that never commits. This is a read-side contract gap distinct from the explicitly acknowledged stale-write semantics. Define a coherent committed read view or a read/retry boundary for graph consumers; the existing single-writer direction need not change.

votes.evidence: Narrowed: the design does state reconciliation's latest-committed-intent behavioral contract (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:15-16; DESIGN-NOTES.md:177-179), so the gap is its missing read boundary, plus /seat's. Reproduction: (1) graph state, templates, overrides, and seat/clone state live in human-readable files in one shared checkout (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:9-10,14,23-25; DESIGN-NOTES.md:28,149-150,202,219). (2) A serialized worker applies a multi-file template/override or name/path mutation and commits it (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:14,23-25; DESIGN-NOTES.md:17-18,58,150); serialization controls writers, but no cited section gives concurrent readers a revision-pinned view or says to wait/retry during that mutation. (3) Separately triggered reconciliation or /seat can read after one file/path changes and before the grouped update commits (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:15,30; DESIGN-NOTES.md:164-165,193,238-239). (4) It can therefore act on a mixture of old and new desired state, or /seat can load an interim path/configuration. Acting on that mixture contradicts the explicit latest committed intent rule (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:16; DESIGN-NOTES.md:179); a /seat load using interim state also fails its latest applicable template/override/rule requirement (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:30; DESIGN-NOTES.md:193,202). This is a possible design-permitted failure, not a claim that the unbuilt implementation already loses data. A coherent committed read or equivalent wait/retry contract remains to specify.

(a) Equivalent: CURRENT-DESIGN.md:15-16 and DESIGN-NOTES.md:179 require reconciliation to follow latest committed intent, so reconciliation has a semantic boundary; no section gives /seat or direct multi-file readers a coherent revision/read-retry mechanism. CURRENT-DESIGN.md:30 and DESIGN-NOTES.md:238-239 instead have the agent read applicable state directly from human-browsable files; DESIGN-NOTES.md:149-150 specifies separate seat/clone files and one serialized writer. (b) Accepted tradeoffs in DESIGN-NOTES.md:153,180 concern non-atomic external effects and missed manual observations, not seeing half of one graph commit. (c) The issue is within scope because load and reconciliation are core operations (HERDR-GRAPH-VISION.md:60,92-98). (d) During a grouped template/rename update (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:23,30), /seat can read a changed file and an unchanged related file before the writer commits, yielding a binding/configuration that matches no committed graph revision; that can misorient a seat or trigger wrong participation. CURRENT-DESIGN.md:14-16 specifies one serialized writer, a separate reconciler, and latest committed intent; :30 makes /seat read applicable state/templates/overrides/rules itself. DESIGN-NOTES.md:149-150,164-165,238-239 confirms separate files, a shared checkout, independent reconciliation, and direct agent reads. Full-text search across all four reviewed docs for snapshot, consistent/coherent read, isolation, lock, retry, commit/revision view and equivalents found no reader boundary; DESIGN-NOTES.md:179's external-action current-intent check states an outcome but no coherent read mechanism. f.claim: Hydration undo does not define whether later reuse of an originally created object or relationship blocks its retirement, despite promising to preserve unrelated later work.
f.location: DESIGN-NOTES.md:285–289; CURRENT-DESIGN.md — Undo.
f.evidence: The approved rule says 'Undo hydration retires objects created by that action and reverses relationships it added; preserve objects merely reused and external project work.' Suppose hydration A creates a seat and participation relationship, and hydration B later explicitly reuses both without changing their fields. Undo A still categorizes the seat as created-by-A and the relationship as added-by-A. Applying that inverse retires the live seat relied on by B; preserving objects reused by A does not protect later reusers of A's creations. Same-field edit conflicts are cited, and exact dependency checks are explicitly left open, but later reuse must be a dependency even where no field differs from A's after-state. Define whether undo rejects, retains, or transfers such shared ownership; creation provenance alone cannot decide a safe inverse.

votes.evidence: Concrete sequence: hydration A creates seat S and adds relationship R; grouped provenance records created/reused seat IDs (DESIGN-NOTES.md:285-286,302). A later, independently selected hydration B reuses S and R without changing a field, which the design permits case by case (DESIGN-NOTES.md:39-40,285-286). The stated inverse for A retires objects A created and reverses relationships A added (DESIGN-NOTES.md:286; CURRENT-DESIGN.md:47-48). Applied literally, it retires S and removes R despite B's continuing use, contradicting the requirement that undo preserve unrelated later work (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:47; DESIGN-NOTES.md:279,287-289). Same-field edit conflict handling does not catch this dependency because B made no edit. Exact dependency conflict checks are acknowledged as unfinished (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:49; DESIGN-NOTES.md:274,289). The finding concerns the missing later-reuse rule, not a claim that the draft implementation already loses state.

(a) No equivalent rule resolves later reuse of an object or relationship created by the selected hydration. DESIGN-NOTES.md:285-289 and CURRENT-DESIGN.md:46-49 record provenance, preview, and agent repair for conflicts, but never say whether reuse without a field edit is a conflict or whether it retains/transfers ownership. DESIGN-NOTES.md:274 expressly leaves exact dependency conflicts open. (b) Best-effort external reconciliation (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:15-17) does not accept loss of unrelated later graph work during undo; the undo contract says preserve it (line 47). (c) Hydration undo is explicitly in initial scope (CURRENT-DESIGN.md:47-48). (d) If A creates seat S and relationship R, then B reuses S and R unchanged, retiring A's creations removes B's still-desired organization. The generic conflict route only helps if this dependency is recognized. This is an acknowledged, material design gap, not evidence of an existing implementation defect.

Grounded, with narrowing: CURRENT-DESIGN.md:25 and DESIGN-NOTES.md:302 say grouped hydration actions reference created/reused seat IDs; CURRENT-DESIGN.md:47-49 and DESIGN-NOTES.md:285-289 approve creation-provenance undo, preserving unrelated work, concrete preview, and routing conflicts for repair. DESIGN-NOTES.md:274,280 and CURRENT-DESIGN.md:49 explicitly leave dependency conflict checks/resolution open. Full-text searches across all four reviewed documents for undo, reuse, dependency, conflict, ownership, adoption, and equivalent mechanisms found no rule for A-created seat/relationship later reused by B without a field edit. If A is undone, the literal create/add inverse can retire a seat and relationship B still relies on; no same-field conflict need exist. This is a material acknowledged design gap in safe hydration undo, not evidence of actual data loss or a demand for a completed implementation. The spec does record B's reused seat ID, so the gap is deciding how that dependency affects preview/inversion, not a claim that detection is impossible; relationship-level reuse/provenance is less explicit. No external premise is needed.

f.claim: Preserving a native transcript while transferring its clone between seats requires historical scope segments, but the attribution contract only names identities and does not define the cutover that separates old-seat work from new-seat work.
f.location: CURRENT-DESIGN.md, Identity and scope / State and reconciliation; DESIGN-NOTES.md:16, 148–149, 230, 256

Narrowed to transcript-derived history: CURRENT-DESIGN.md:9,19 requires seat/clone/session/transcript attribution and preserves a clone's old transcript through a cross-tab move while changing applicable state. Thus one continuing transcript can cover seat A and seat B; mapping its clone only to its present seat would relabel the A portion, and a result covering both portions has no defined scope attribution. f.claim: The transcript result contract cannot yet distinguish a fully summarized prefix from disjoint completed ranges, so accepting an out-of-order processed-through result can conceal an unprocessed gap.
f.location: CURRENT-DESIGN.md, Bootstrap and system-duty seats; DESIGN-NOTES.md:248, 251, 256–259
f.evidence: Results reference transcript identity, a processed-through position and an output artifact; resumed transcripts generate processing for newly appended portions, and the summarizer dispatches concurrently. The notes explicitly leave concurrent/out-of-order result handling open. Concrete case: request A covers the existing prefix through position 100; a resume adds positions 101–200 and request B completes first. If the stored frontier becomes 200, A's missing prefix is hidden; if it stays below 100, graph needs some other record of B's completed range to avoid rescheduling or losing its artifact.
